parts: Lesson 23: Molecular Inheritance and Gene Expression — Summary
One gene one enzyme and DNA as genetic material

Garrod described inborn errors of metabolism (phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria) caused by absent enzymes. Beadle and Tatum, working on Neurospora mutants, proposed the one gene-one enzyme hypothesis (later one gene-one polypeptide). Griffith (1928) showed bacterial transformation in Streptococcus pneumoniae: heat-killed virulent smooth (S) cells mixed with harmless rough (R) cells made the R cells virulent. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944) showed that DNA was the transforming principle (DNase destroyed the effect). Hershey and Chase (1952) used T2 bacteriophage: radioactive sulphur-35 labelled the protein coat and stayed outside; radioactive phosphorus-32 labelled the viral DNA and entered the bacteria, proving that DNA is the genetic material.

DNA is a polynucleotide; each nucleotide has three subunits: a pentose sugar (deoxyribose), a nitrogenous base (purines adenine and guanine; pyrimidines thymine and cytosine) and a phosphate group. Base + sugar = nucleoside; base + sugar + phosphate = nucleotide. Chargaff's rule: A = T and G = C (purines equal pyrimidines). Watson and Crick (1953; Nobel prize; X-ray data of Franklin and Wilkins) double helix model: two antiparallel strands (5' to 3' and 3' to 5') coiled around each other, a sugar-phosphate backbone, bases linked by hydrogen bonds (two between A and T, three between G and C), one turn of 3.4 nm contains 10 base pairs 0.34 nm apart, diameter 2 nm. Packaging in eukaryotes: DNA wound around a histone octamer forms a nucleosome (beads on a string), then the solenoid and supercoils, forming the chromosome.

DNA versus RNA: deoxyribose versus ribose sugar; thymine versus uracil; double-stranded versus mostly single-stranded; DNA carries hereditary information and can duplicate itself while RNA has many types (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) and is synthesised on a DNA template. RNA types: mRNA (copy of a gene; carries the message from the nucleus to the ribosomes), tRNA (clover-leaf shape; anticodon loop recognises the codon; carries a specific amino acid; 3' end CCA) and rRNA (component of ribosomes; role in protein synthesis).

Conjugation (plasmid or F-factor passes from an F+ to an F- cell; Hfr strain), transformation (uptake of extracellular DNA, as in Streptococcus) and transduction (transfer of DNA through a bacteriophage).

Replication occurs in the S-phase and is semiconservative (each new molecule has one old and one new strand; shown by Meselson and Stahl) and semidiscontinuous. Helicase unwinds the strands and topoisomerase keeps them open (replication fork); primase makes an RNA primer (5-10 bases) giving a 3'-OH; DNA polymerase adds nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction; the leading strand is synthesised continuously and the lagging strand discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, which are joined by DNA ligase using ATP; proof-reading corrects errors.

Central dogma: DNA (transcription) → RNA (translation) → protein; in retroviruses RNA → DNA by reverse transcriptase. Genetic code (Nirenberg, Mathaei and Ochoa): triplet (codon), unambiguous, non-overlapping and commaless, degenerate (64 codons for 20 amino acids; wobble hypothesis), universal; AUG codes for methionine and is the initiation (start) codon; UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. A cistron is a gene coding for one polypeptide. Anticodons are complementary to codons: AGU pairs with UCA and UGC with ACG; anticodon GAU pairs with codon CUA.

Transcription: the DNA double helix unwinds (helicase, topoisomerase) and RNA polymerase (starting at the promoter signalled by the sigma factor, stopping with the Rho factor) makes mRNA complementary to the sense strand. In eukaryotes hnRNA is processed: introns are removed and exons joined (splicing), a methyl guanosine cap is added at the 5' end and a poly-A tail at the 3' end before it leaves the nucleus. Translation: amino acid activation by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase using ATP; initiation (mRNA binds to the small ribosomal subunit, methionine tRNA attaches to the AUG codon); elongation (peptidyl transferase forms peptide bonds; the ribosome moves along mRNA toward the 3' end); polysome (several ribosomes on one mRNA); termination at a stop codon; the polypeptide is released.
Regulation of gene expression and mutation

Housekeeping genes are expressed all the time; inducible genes are switched on by a substance and repressible genes are switched off. Lac operon (Jacob and Monod, E. coli): regulator gene i, promoter p, operator o and structural genes z, y, a (galactosidase, permease, transacetylase); in the absence of lactose the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription; lactose (inducer) binds the repressor, which releases the operator, and the genes are switched on. Mutation: a sudden heritable change in the genetic material; gene (point) mutations (substitution, deletion, insertion, frame shift) and chromosomal mutations; caused by mutagens such as radiation and chemicals; harmful effects include genetic disorders and cancer while useful ones give variation for evolution and new varieties in crops.
